cards.title: Pharmacological Inhibition of MAPK Signaling Attenuates LSD-Induced Hallucinogenic-like Effects and Differentially Modulates Persistent Behavioral and Structural Plasticity in Mice
cards.post: Aim: To test whether MAPK/ERK signalling contributes to the acute and persistent effects of LSD in male mice. Methods: Male mice received LSD with the brain-penetrant MEK inhibitor SL327 at several doses. Outcomes included immediate early gene expression, head-twitch response, forced-swim immobility and dendritic spine density in frontal cortex, with some analyses of beta-arrestin-2 knockouts. Results: SL327 dose-dependently attenuated LSD-induced c-Fos, Egr-1 and Egr-2 expression and markedly reduced acute head twitches without altering locomotion. LSD reduced thin spine density at 24 h and 7 days and increased mushroom spine density at 7 days; MAPK inhibition prevented the thin spine reduction. Conclusion: MAPK/ERK signalling contributes to psychedelic-specific transcription and acute and delayed LSD responses, with a spine-subtype-dependent role in cortical plasticity. Male-only sampling limits generalisation to females.
cards.why_you: Speaks directly to LSD's plasticity and 5-HT2A signalling, the neuroplastogen questions behind your multimodal plasticity work.

cards.title: DMT-induced aberrant salience and suggestibility correlate with mystical experiences and positive emotionality
cards.post: Aim: To test whether DMT-induced aberrant salience and suggestibility relate to mystical and emotional psychedelic experiences. Methods: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind crossover study in 25 healthy participants receiving inhaled DMT (60 mg) or active placebo (0.6 mg), with aberrant salience, suggestibility and psychedelic experience questionnaires. Results: Compared with placebo, DMT increased all aberrant salience factors, most suggestibility modalities and most psychedelic factors. Aberrant salience correlated widely with psychedelic experiences, particularly mystical and positive emotional factors. Conclusion: DMT induces both psychosis- and therapy-relevant processes, with the link to mystical experience possibly indirect and emotionality playing a more central role.
cards.why_you: Adds DMT evidence to the psychedelic clinical pharmacology strand, linking suggestibility and emotion to the mystical experiences your DMT work touches.

cards.title: Working memory neural correlates after ketamine in treatment-resistant depression: a randomized placebo-controlled functional magnetic resonance imaging study.
cards.post: Aim: To examine working memory behaviour and fMRI activation after ketamine in treatment-resistant depression versus healthy volunteers. Methods: Secondary analysis of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 22 unmedicated treatment-resistant depression participants and 19 healthy volunteers, given ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) or placebo with 3T fMRI during an N-back task. Results: Ketamine significantly reduced depression scores versus placebo (p < 0.01), but N-back performance did not differ by drug condition. Region-specific activation changes were observed, including reduced parieto-occipital junction activation after ketamine. Conclusion: Ketamine's antidepressant effect occurred without significant working memory change, though task-related regional changes were seen. Modest sample size and exploratory ROI analyses limit interpretation.
cards.why_you: Relevant to your ketamine neuroimaging work and EEG and fMRI methods, though this is a modest exploratory analysis rather than a plasticity study.

cards.title: Multimodal PET/MR imaging in Alzheimer's disease: A comparative study of structural, metabolic, synaptic and perfusion measures.
cards.venue: European journal of nuclear medicine and molecular imaging
cards.post: Aim: To compare structural, metabolic, synaptic and perfusion PET/MR measures for detecting neurodegeneration and discriminating Alzheimer's disease from healthy volunteers. Methods: 36 biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer's patients underwent 18F-FDG, 18F-SynVesT-1 (SV2A) PET/MR and neuropsychological testing, with cortical thickness, ASL perfusion and volumetry compared against a healthy cohort using cross-validated classification. Results: 18F-FDG PET showed large reductions and the best discrimination (AUC 0.94). Cortical thickness, SV2A PET and volumetry gave similar performance (AUC 0.81-0.86), while ASL was weakest (AUC 0.72) and absent in MCI. Conclusion: Multimodal measures show overlapping but distinct patterns, with synaptic and structural abnormalities present in MCI and perfusion deficits emerging only in dementia-stage disease.
cards.why_you: Directly applies SV2A PET and PET-MR methods you use, benchmarking synaptic density imaging against established biomarkers.

cards.title: Psychedelic-assisted therapies (Psilocybin and MDMA) for treatment-resistant psychiatric disorders
cards.post: Aim: To describe the mechanisms, efficacy and safety of psilocybin- and MDMA-assisted therapy for depression and PTSD, and to critically examine evidence limitations. Methods: Narrative, non-systematic review of PubMed/MEDLINE literature from 2016 onwards, including randomised trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses and mechanistic and safety studies; twelve references were qualitatively synthesised. Results: Psilocybin reduced depressive symptoms with a moderate pooled effect (Hedges' g = 0.66), with limited evidence specific to treatment-resistant depression. MDMA-assisted therapy reduced PTSD severity in two phase 3 trials, with transient adverse effects common and serious events reported in people with neuropsychiatric conditions. Conclusion: Psychedelic-assisted therapies are promising but methodological limits, safety uncertainties and unclear long-term efficacy warrant caution before wider implementation.
cards.why_you: Summarises the psilocybin depression evidence base that your clinical pharmacology and psilocybin work sits within.

cards.title: Roots to Thrive risk and readiness assessment: a practice-based intake and decision-support framework for psychedelic-assisted therapy.
cards.post: Aim: To develop and describe a trauma-informed readiness and risk assessment framework for community-based psychedelic-assisted therapy intake. Methods: Multi-year practice-based quality improvement process from 2020 within a community psychedelic-assisted therapy programme and a university graduate setting, using iterative clinical application, consultation and feedback. Results: The framework integrates biomedical, psychological, relational, cultural, ecological and transpersonal domains to support contextual intake decisions, with reported gains in shared language and alignment with community practice. Conclusion: The framework shifts screening from exclusion towards readiness and risk matched to supports, though it is not yet psychometrically validated and was developed in one setting.
cards.why_you: Relevant to the translation and governance side of psychedelic therapy, a practice-based view that sits beside your clinical pharmacology interests.

cards.title: Mescaline enhances emotional empathy via 5-HT2A receptor activation.
cards.post: Aim: To assess the acute effects of several mescaline doses on empathy and plasma oxytocin, and the role of 5-HT2A receptors. Methods: Placebo-controlled, double-blind crossover study in 16 healthy participants receiving placebo, mescaline 100, 200, 400 and 800 mg, and 800 mg mescaline with the 5-HT2A antagonist ketanserin, using the Multifaceted Empathy Test and plasma oxytocin. Results: Mescaline dose-dependently enhanced emotional empathy and reduced cognitive empathy, and raised plasma oxytocin significantly only at 400 and 800 mg. Ketanserin blocked the empathy and oxytocin effects. Conclusion: Classic psychedelics acutely alter empathy and oxytocin through 5-HT2A receptor interaction, providing further evidence for this mechanism.
cards.why_you: Links 5-HT2A receptor activation to social and emotional processing, relevant to your interest in brain-body and interoceptive effects of psychedelics.

cards.title: The "dark magic mushroom" co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin.
cards.post: Aim: To determine whether the mushroom Galerina indica produces both psilocybin and amatoxins. Methods: Mass spectrometry of mushroom tissue to detect psilocybin and amatoxins, genomic analysis to identify biosynthetic genes, and phylogenetic analysis to infer their evolutionary origin. Results: Psilocybin and amatoxins were both detected, with corresponding biosynthetic genes identified. Phylogenetic evidence suggests psilocybin biosynthesis was acquired by horizontal gene transfer after amatoxin biosynthesis was established. Conclusion: Horizontal gene transfer can combine bioactive systems in one species, potentially altering the ecological roles and fitness of both compound classes.
cards.why_you: Of limited direct relevance to your PET or neurodynamics work, though it touches psilocybin chemistry you may find of interest.

cards.title: Levetiracetam, brivaracetam and piracetam at D₂ and 5-HT₂A receptors: a molecular docking and dynamics investigation.
cards.post: Aim: To test whether levetiracetam, brivaracetam and piracetam engage dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, possibly explaining neuropsychiatric side effects. Methods: Molecular docking into D2 and 5-HT2A orthosteric pockets, followed by three independent 50 ns explicit-membrane molecular dynamics replicates per system (18 trajectories in total). Results: Ligands stayed bound in all frames, but per-residue contacts varied widely between replicates. Occupancy of the pocket was sustained by hydrophobic contact, notably Leu229 at 5-HT2A, in 49-74% of frames. Conclusion: Whether these interactions are pharmacologically meaningful requires radioligand binding measurement rather than further simulation.
cards.why_you: Computational pharmacology of receptor binding parallels your molecular dynamics work on tryptamines, though it is outside your core psychedelic focus.

cards.title: Novel quantification method for psilocin in brain tissues using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry.
cards.venue: Analytical methods : advancing methods and applications
cards.post: Aim: Develops and validates an LC-MS/MS method to quantify psilocin and 4-HIAA in brain tissue. Methods: Chromatography-centred LC-MS/MS approach with matrix dilution, shallower gradient and diverter-valve timing, applied to mouse brain sections from psilocybin and psilocin co-crystal dosing. Results: The method reached a 0.05 ng/mL LLOQ and met validation criteria; no sex or region differences in brain psilocin were found, and psilocybin gave higher psilocin at 10 min than the co-crystal. 4-HIAA was not detected. Conclusion: The validated method enables reliable psilocin quantification in brain tissue, supporting pharmacokinetic work, though the co-crystal difference was not significant.
cards.why_you: A validated brain-tissue psilocin assay would directly support pharmacokinetic characterisation relevant to your psilocybin and tryptamine work.

cards.title: A Pharmacological Basis for Some Bad LSD "Trips"?
cards.post: Aim: Tests whether a metabolite of LSD explains the delayed paranoid phase of LSD intoxication. Methods: Synthesis of 13- and 14-hydroxy-LSD and in vitro receptor testing at the human dopamine D4 receptor. Results: 13-hydroxy-LSD was about 380 times more potent than LSD at the D4 receptor (EC50 36 pM versus 14 nM). Conclusion: 13-hydroxy-LSD may contribute to the delayed dopaminergic phase of LSD action, but in vivo formation and central effects remain unknown.
cards.why_you: Offers a receptor-level hypothesis for the delayed phase of LSD action that bears on your interest in dopaminergic and serotonergic psychedelic pharmacology.

cards.title: Longitudinal [¹⁸F]FDG PET changes map onto distinct cholinergic and serotonergic territories in autoimmune encephalitis.
cards.venue: European journal of nuclear medicine and molecular imaging
cards.post: Aim: Tests whether longitudinal [18F]FDG PET changes in autoimmune encephalitis align with specific neuromodulatory receptor territories. Methods: Retrospective secondary analysis of 22 patients with baseline and follow-up FDG PET, using JuSpace spatial correlation with 15 normative neurotransmitter maps and permutation-based inference with FDR correction. Results: Metabolic change correlated positively with VAChT (q = 0.023) and alpha4beta2 (q = 0.004) maps and negatively with 5-HT2A (q = 0.014). No clinical associations survived multiplicity correction. Conclusion: Metabolic change maps onto cholinergic and serotonergic territories, generating hypotheses about recovery, though spatial overlap does not imply directional signalling.
cards.why_you: Applies receptor-space PET correlation methods akin to your serotonin PET and synaptic density work.

cards.title: 5-HT2A receptor deletion is associated with reduced hippocampal parvalbumin levels and anxiety-like behavior in BALB/c mice
cards.post: Aim: Investigates whether constitutive loss of 5-HT2A receptors alters anxiety-like behaviour and hippocampal parvalbumin interneuron proteins in BALB/c mice. Methods: Constitutive 5-HT2AR knockout in male and female BALB/c mice, behavioural anxiety paradigms, unbiased hippocampal proteomics, and perineuronal net component analysis; a separate cohort received the 5-HT2AR agonist 25CN-NBOH. Results: Knockout mice showed robust anxiety-like and repetitive behaviour, with reduced hippocampal parvalbumin and energy-metabolism proteins, and reduced HAPLN4, while aggrecan and HAPLN1 were unchanged. Conclusion: Loss of 5-HT2AR signalling is associated with coordinated reductions in parvalbumin and bioenergetic machinery without generalised loss of perineuronal net components.
cards.why_you: Connects 5-HT2A signalling to parvalbumin interneurons, relevant to the anxiolytic mechanisms of psychedelics you study.

cards.title: Lysergic Acid Diethylamide Induces Transcriptional Changes Opposing Signatures of Brain Ageing and Neurodegeneration.
cards.post: Aim: Asks whether LSD-induced transcriptional changes oppose gene expression signatures of brain ageing and dementia. Methods: Cross-species transcriptomic analysis of chronic LSD in rats and acute LSD in mice, compared with human prefrontal cortex ageing and dementia datasets, plus amyloid-beta experiments in primary cortical cultures. Results: LSD-induced profiles were strongly anti-correlated with human ageing signatures and, less strongly, with dementia signatures, and short-term LSD attenuated amyloid-beta-induced alterations. Conclusion: Provides a transcriptional rationale for investigating LSD and related compounds in brain ageing and neurodegeneration, pointing to mechanisms for future study.

cards.title: Psilocybin-Assisted Therapy for Cancer-Related Psychological and Existential Distress in Adults with Cancer: An Integrative Systematic Review.
cards.venue: Journal of pain & palliative care pharmacotherapy
cards.post: Aim: Evaluates evidence on the safety, efficacy and therapeutic impact of psilocybin-assisted therapy for cancer-related psychological and existential distress. Methods: Integrative systematic review following PRISMA guidelines of 11 reports from six clinical cohorts, searched August to October 2025, with MMAT appraisal. Results: Single moderate-to-high psilocybin doses produced rapid, enduring reductions in depression, anxiety and existential distress lasting 2 to 6 months, and up to 4.5 years in some cases; no serious adverse events were reported. Conclusion: Psilocybin-assisted therapy may be promising for cancer-related distress but remains investigational, with several reports showing methodological limitations.

cards.venue: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
cards.post: Aim: Tests whether Scn2a deficiency alters behavioural responses to psilocybin and serotonergic system function in mice. Methods: Scn2a-deficient and wild-type mice given psilocybin, assessed for sociability, anxiety-like behaviour and head twitch response, with mPFC serotonin levels and receptor expression, and dorsal raphe nucleus firing measured. Conclusion: Scn2a deficiency is associated with serotonergic alterations and differential psilocybin responses, suggesting serotonergic interventions may ameliorate social deficits in SCN2A-related autism.

cards.title: Integrating Transformative and Existential Strategies into Trauma-Focused Psychotherapy: A Multi-Study Analysis of EMDR, 3MDR, and Psychedelic-Assisted Group Therapy
cards.venue: ERA: Education and Research Archive (University of Alberta)
cards.post: Aim: To test whether transformation strategies within trauma therapies help patients reach deeper existential aspects of suffering, and how interpersonal interaction and transformation contribute to accessing deeper pain and meaning. Methods: Thesis combining a secondary qualitative analysis of 18 psychiatric outpatients with suicidal ideation treated with 12 sessions of web-based EMDR, and a mixed-methods single case study of 3MDR for PTSD in a person with dissociative identity disorder, with follow-up interviews. Results: Three existential themes emerged in the EMDR cohort: self-against-self, the anguish of being, and existential despair. In the 3MDR case, PTSD, anxiety and depression scores improved, with reported resolution of existential themes and post-traumatic growth. Conclusion: The authors suggest many people with chronic suicidality face existential crises rarely addressed in manualised therapies, and that adapted, transformative approaches may be needed. Findings come from a small sample and a single case.

cards.title: The spatial distribution of glioblastoma correlates with specific neurotransmitter maps
cards.post: Aim: To test whether the spatial distribution of glioblastoma follows the normative neurotransmitter and receptor architecture of the healthy brain. Methods: Retrospective study of 96 glioblastoma patients (mean age 62.2 years) from Padova University Hospital, with parcel-wise lesion frequency maps compared to normative PET neurotransmitter maps across two atlases using Neuromaps and spatially constrained null models. Results: Glioblastoma frequency correlated with dopaminergic, serotonergic and cholinergic systems, including 5-HT4 (ρ = 0.57, qFDR = 0.028), D2/D3 (ρ = 0.62, qFDR = 0.029) and DAT (r = 0.47, qFDR = 0.003). Higher expression of these neurotransmitters was associated with more frequent tumour occurrence. Conclusion: The authors conclude that the brain's neurochemical architecture may contribute to the spatial distribution of gliomas, consistent with gliomas integrating into functional neural networks. The design is correlational.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your PET neurotransmitter mapping work, applying normative receptor maps to a clinical spatial question.

cards.title: Cortical Hypoperfusion in Acute Anorexia Nervosa Is Graded Along the Sensorimotor-Association Hierarchy.
cards.venue: The International journal of eating disorders
cards.post: Aim: To determine whether cortical hypoperfusion in acute anorexia nervosa is uniform or organised along the cortex's principal functional gradient, and whether it dissociates from cortical thinning. Methods: 44 acutely underweight women with anorexia nervosa and 45 healthy women underwent 3T pseudo-continuous arterial spin labelling with partial-volume correction, analysed across the Schaefer 100-region atlas and compared with cortical thickness and 18 PET/SPECT receptor maps. Results: Perfusion was lower in 97 of 100 regions, maximal in orbitofrontal and prefrontal cortex (composite d = -0.56). The deficit scaled with position along the principal functional gradient (ρ = -0.56), and hypoperfusion was greater where D1, CB1, mGluR5, M1, 5-HT2A and μ-opioid systems are dense. Conclusion: Cortical hypoperfusion in acute anorexia nervosa is graded along the sensorimotor-association axis, dissociable from thinning and aligned with reward-related neurochemistry. The cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

cards.title: Changes in wellbeing, self-compassion and alexithymia in a proof of principle trial with MDMA-assisted therapy for major depressive disorder.
cards.post: Aim: To examine whether MDMA-assisted therapy changes alexithymia, self-compassion and well-being in major depressive disorder, and whether effects last. Methods: Open-label proof-of-principle trial with 12 participants with moderate to severe MDD (baseline MADRS 29.6), receiving two MDMA sessions with manualised psychotherapy; outcomes at baseline, 8 weeks and at least 3 months, analysed with linear mixed models. Results: TAS-20 fell by 11.75 post-treatment and 16.42 at follow-up (both p < 0.001). Self-compassion rose (SCS +0.73, p = 0.017; +1.07 at follow-up, p = 0.001). WEMWBS improved by 17.30 at both timepoints (p < 0.001). Conclusion: The authors conclude MDMA-assisted therapy produced lasting gains in alexithymia, self-compassion and well-being beyond symptom reduction. The trial is open-label, small and without a control group.

cards.title: Sample size critically shapes the reliability of EEG case-control findings in psychiatry.
cards.post: Aim: Quantify how sample size affects the reliability of EEG case-control findings across psychiatric conditions in children and adolescents. Methods: Resting-state EEG from 2,874 participants aged 5–18 years, including ADHD, autism, anxiety, learning disorders and controls, with spectral, temporal and complexity features compared across repeated random subsamples of varying size. Results: Small samples gave unstable, inflated and highly variable effect sizes, while larger samples converged on consistent but small effects. Statistical power rose steeply with sample size, while false positive rates stayed relatively stable. Conclusion: Sample size critically shapes EEG case-control outcomes, and conventional case-control designs may be limited for biomarker discovery in psychiatry.
cards.why_you: Directly addresses the reliability of EEG complexity measures in psychiatric case-control designs, central to your EEG complexity and computational psychiatry work.

cards.title: Efficacy Evaluation of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation at Individual Frequency for Patients With Prolonged Disorders of Consciousness: A Preliminary Study Based on Mismatch Negative Amplitude.
cards.post: Aim: To test whether rTMS at an individually selected frequency, guided by mismatch negativity amplitude, improves consciousness in prolonged disorders of consciousness. Methods: Double-blind randomised controlled study of 29 patients; experimental group received individual frequency selection (5, 10 or 15 Hz) based on optimal MMN response, controls received fixed 10 Hz; 4 weeks of rTMS targeting the left mastoid alongside routine rehabilitation. Results: All groups improved. The 15 Hz group (n = 7) had the largest gains (CRS-R 4.71 to 9.29), with greater net improvement than controls (Z = -1.998, p = 0.046). MMN amplitude increased in the 5 Hz and 10 Hz experimental subgroups versus controls. Conclusion: The authors suggest individualised rTMS frequency guided by MMN may aid consciousness recovery and that MMN may be an objective biomarker. The very small subgroups and preliminary design limit inference.
cards.why_you: Connects TMS and EEG-based biomarkers, a direct overlap with your TMS-EEG and neurodynamics methods.

cards.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans.
cards.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
cards.post: Aim: To determine how single-pulse TMS to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex affects single-neuron activity in deep cortical and subcortical structures in humans. Methods: Intracranial microelectrode recordings of 185 single neurons in four neurosurgical patients during single-pulse TMS to left dlPFC, with artifact cleaning enabling spike resolution from 8 ms, alongside TMS-evoked potentials from depth macroelectrodes. Results: Single-pulse TMS elicited time-locked responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated, 19% suppressed, 1% both), in putamen and thalamus among other regions. Putative inhibitory striato-thalamic neurons were facilitated, while excitatory and limbic neurons were suppressed with slower time courses. Conclusion: The authors propose dlPFC TMS recruits many neurons across bilateral cortical and subcortical regions, selectively boosting inhibitory firing in executive networks while suppressing limbic drive. Data come from four patients.
cards.why_you: Directly addresses how TMS perturbs neural circuits at single-neuron resolution, central to your TMS-EEG and whole-brain modelling interests.

cards.title: Functional and structural neuroplasticity of motor system in hemiplegic cerebral palsy
cards.post: Aim: To characterise structural and functional reorganisation of the motor system in hemiplegic cerebral palsy and its links to lesion characteristics and upper-limb performance. Methods: 26 children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy and 26 typically developing controls; electromagnetic source imaging of movement-related oscillations, navigated TMS for corticospinal excitability and lateralisation, and functionally guided diffusion MRI; Melbourne Assessment 2 and correlation, latent-variable and mediation analyses. Results: Descending and commissural fibres showed lower fractional anisotropy and higher diffusivity. TMS identified ipsilateral corticospinal projections from the less affected hemisphere in 17 of 22 children. Larger lesions were associated with poorer motor performance (Rho -0.74 to -0.57). Conclusion: The authors suggest developmental neuroplasticity and reorganisation of motor pathways contribute to variable motor outcomes despite similar lesions. The study is cross-sectional and the preprint is not yet peer reviewed.

cards.title: An Integrated Chronic Cisterna Magna Access Preparation for Glymphatic MRI in Awake and Mechanically Ventilated Anesthetized Mice.
cards.post: Aim: To describe a standardised mouse preparation enabling intracisternal tracer delivery and dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI across awake and anaesthetised states. Methods: Chronic cisterna magna catheter mechanically linked to an implanted head holder; graded habituation for awake imaging; intubation and mechanical ventilation for anaesthetised imaging; serial 3D T1-weighted imaging during intracisternal Gd-DTPA infusion. Results: Representative data show stable intracisternal access, manageable motion in awake acquisition, and interpretable spatiotemporal signal changes under awake, isoflurane and ketamine/xylazine conditions. No quantitative comparison is reported. Conclusion: The authors suggest the framework will support comparative and longitudinal studies of CSF tracer transport across physiological and anaesthetic conditions. It is a methods protocol with representative rather than statistical data.

cards.title: SV2A PET imaging in Parkinson's disease and atypical parkinsonism: A systematic review of neuroimaging methodologies and regional findings.
cards.post: Aim: To review neuroimaging methods and regional findings from SV2A PET in Parkinson's disease and atypical parkinsonian disorders. Methods: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020 of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science; 14 studies using validated SV2A PET radiotracers in parkinsonian populations; risk of bias with QUADAS-2; narrative synthesis as heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis. Results: In PD the substantia nigra was most affected, with striatal involvement in advanced disease. In PSP and CBD synaptic loss was widespread and exceeded grey matter atrophy, falling about 3-4% per year in some longitudinal regions. In MSA infratentorial involvement predominated, with AUC up to 0.99. Conclusion: The authors conclude SV2A PET shows disease-specific presynaptic patterns supporting its use as a diagnostic and monitoring biomarker. They call for methodological harmonisation and longitudinal multicentre studies.

cards.title: Novel SV2A PET/MRI reveals mechanism behind whole brain synaptic density changes during radiation therapy for treatment of brain tumors
cards.post: Aim: Identify an early imaging biomarker of synaptic change after whole-brain radiation, to predict cognitive decline in a rodent model. Methods: Seventy-two Sprague-Dawley rats underwent baseline and follow-up SV2A PET (18F-SynVesT-1) and DTI MRI after 3 Gy x 10 fractions of whole-brain, hemisphere or sham irradiation, with kinetic modelling and Western blotting. Results: Irradiated regions showed increased tracer uptake at 1 month, with hippocampal DVR of 1.5 versus 1.34 in non-irradiated tissue (p < 0.05), similar changes in frontal, insular and amygdala regions. Differences disappeared at 3 and 6 months, and R1 and diffusion measures were unchanged. Conclusion: The authors conclude that SV2A PET is an early biomarker of radiation-induced synaptic change that may predict cognitive outcome, though this rests on a rodent model.

cards.title: Multidimensional Electrophysiological Responses to TMS on the Primary Motor Cortex: A TMS-EEG Characterization of Immediate Cortical Responses
cards.post: Aim: Compare immediate cortical responses to 10 Hz rTMS, 1 Hz rTMS and iTBS over the primary motor cortex using TMS-EEG. Methods: Randomised within-subject crossover study in 17 healthy adults receiving three stimulation protocols in separate sessions, with TEPs, power spectral density and EEG microstate dynamics assessed before and after stimulation. cards.title: Bayesian Kinetic Model Selection in Dynamic PET via Consistency Models
cards.post: Aim: Perform voxel-wise Bayesian kinetic model selection and parameter estimation in dynamic PET using consistency models, faster than MCMC. Methods: Consistency model sampling the joint posterior over kinetic parameters and model index, validated in simulations and clinical whole-body [18F]FDG total-body PET and brain [11C]raclopride PET. Results: Model selection accuracy was 97.97% for [18F]FDG (versus 58.67% for NLS+AIC) and 91.4% for [11C]raclopride (versus 73.5% for NLS+BIC), with parameter posteriors closely matching MCMC; smoking-induced dopamine release was mapped in the brain. Conclusion: The authors conclude the framework enables fast, accurate Bayesian kinetic model selection across whole-body and brain PET, though validation is limited to the tracers studied.

cards.post: Aim: Test whether immediate TMS-evoked EEG potentials give a more direct measure of short-latency intracortical inhibition than MEP-based SICI. cards.title: Methylphenidate-associated brain structural changes and neuroimaging predictors of treatment response in youth with ADHD: a systematic review.
cards.post: Aim: Review how long-term methylphenidate treatment relates to brain structure, and whether baseline imaging predicts treatment response, in youth with ADHD. cards.title: Concurrent neuronal activity gates persistent dendritic spine shrinkage during mGluR-induced long-term depression
cards.post: Aim: To determine whether mGluR-dependent long-term depression is accompanied by persistent dendritic spine shrinkage, and what conditions govern this coupling. Methods: Organotypic rat hippocampal slice cultures; mGluR-LTD induced with the mGluR1/5 agonist DHPG; spine morphology and calcium transients monitored in CA1 pyramidal neurons; pharmacological manipulations and two-photon glutamate uncaging. Results: Persistent long-term spine shrinkage occurred with mGluR activation only under elevated neuronal activity, termed MIND-sLTD. It required mGluR1/5 and protein synthesis but not NMDA receptor signalling, and single-spine shrinkage was induced when mGluR activation was synchronised with glutamate uncaging. Conclusion: mGluR activation coincident with synaptic activity drives persistent structural depression, suggesting a coincidence-detection mechanism for long-term spine remodelling.

cards.title: Negative allosteric modulation of α5-GABAA receptors engages dynamic cortical glutamatergic and GABAergic mechanisms underlying adaptive behavior in mice.
cards.post: Aim: To test whether negative allosteric modulation of α5-GABAA receptors with basmisanil produces ketamine-like antidepressant actions via specific medial prefrontal cortex cell populations. Methods: Mice exposed to chronic stress; behavioural testing of motivation, hedonia and coping; c-Fos ensemble mapping; signalling and synaptic protein analyses; chemogenetic silencing of CaMKII pyramidal neurons and GABAergic interneurons at different time points. Results: Basmisanil rapidly and durably facilitated behaviour and reversed chronic stress deficits. It preferentially recruited D1R- and SST-expressing cells, increased Erk and Akt-mTOR signalling and synaptic proteins, and early pyramidal silencing blocked both rapid and sustained effects while interneuron silencing blocked sustained effects. Conclusion: Early pyramidal activation initiates rapid plasticity, whereas GABAergic interneurons sustain and express the lasting antidepressant-like effects, highlighting interneuron circuits as targets.

cards.post: Aim: To characterise longitudinal peripheral blood transcriptional changes during ECT and serial ketamine treatment in treatment-resistant depression. Methods: Peripheral blood RNA-seq in 37 ECT patients, 60 ketamine patients and 35 controls at multiple time points; differential expression and WGCNA co-expression network analysis with multiple-comparison correction. cards.title: Intravenous ketamine for major depressive episodes in routine practice: a review of non-randomized evidence on effectiveness and safety.
cards.post: Aim: To review non-randomised evidence on the effectiveness and safety of intravenous racemic ketamine for major depressive episodes in routine practice. Methods: Systematic searches of PubMed, Embase and PsycINFO to 30 September 2026; 56 non-randomised studies included. Results: Response ranged from 26% to 71% and remission from 14% to 53%, overlapping RCT estimates. Benefits often waned within weeks, attrition was high, blood pressure rises were transient, and serious adverse events and urinary and hepatic outcomes were poorly reported. Conclusion: Durability of benefit and cumulative safety of repeated IV ketamine remain uncertain; systematic safety monitoring and head-to-head and maintenance trials are needed.

cards.title: Beyond Side Effects: The Role of Dissociation in Esketamine Therapy for Treatment-Resistant Depression.
cards.venue: Journal of trauma & dissociation : the official journal of the International Society for the Study of Dissociation (ISSD)
cards.post: Aim: To examine whether dissociation during intranasal esketamine therapy affects depressive outcomes in treatment-resistant depression. Methods: Retrospective chart review of 51 adults at an Israeli esketamine unit (2021-2025); DES-II trait dissociation, weekly PDEQ state dissociation, QIDS-SR16 severity; correlations and linear mixed-effects models. Results: Higher trait dissociation was associated with greater baseline depressive severity (r = .28, p = .03) but did not change the pace or magnitude of improvement. cards.post: Aim: To evaluate combined palmitoylethanolamide and probiotic supplementation on behaviour and hippocampal and colonic gene expression in middle-aged mice exposed to chronic stress. cards.title: Proteomic profiling of postmortem prefrontal cortex identifies molecular signatures of borderline personality disorder
cards.post: Aim: To characterise proteomic signatures of borderline personality disorder in postmortem prefrontal cortex. Methods: Label-free proteomics of postmortem prefrontal cortex in 79 individuals (36 with BPD, 43 controls); differential expression, co-expression network, druggability and drug-repositioning analyses; integration with PTSD and MDD datasets. Results: Dysregulation of mitochondrial, immunological and neuroplasticity pathways was observed. A BPD-associated module enriched for secretory and synaptic processes was druggable by SSRIs, and STX7 and RTN4 were conserved differentially expressed proteins across BPD, PTSD and MDD. Conclusion: The study provides initial proteomic insights into BPD in the brain, suggests VEGF signalling as a possible target, and shows convergent signatures with common comorbidities.

cards.title: Abnormalities and plasticity of white matter functional networks in opioid use disorder: a BOLD fMRI study.
cards.post: Aim: To investigate architecture and activity of white matter functional networks in opioid use disorder and their change after prolonged abstinence. Methods: BOLD fMRI white matter signals analysed with k-means clustering in individuals with OUD at baseline and follow-up after prolonged abstinence, compared with healthy controls. Results: At baseline the deep frontoparietal network fragmented into the superior longitudinal fasciculus and anterior corona radiata networks, partially recovering after abstinence. Hyperactivation in the deep frontal network and hypoactivation in the frontotemporal-parietal network were present, with the latter negatively correlated with years of opioid use. Conclusion: OUD disrupts white matter network architecture and activity, while prolonged abstinence promotes partial restoration, indicating neuroplastic potential of white matter networks.

cards.post: Aim: To test whether brain aging, measured as a brain age gap, is elevated in medication-free people with major depressive disorder and whether it depends on age and neuroanatomical phenotype. Methods: Harmonised T1-weighted MRI from 645 medication-free people with a current depressive episode and 645 matched healthy controls across 11 sites; gradient boosting brain age estimation with nested cross-validation and SHAP regional contributions. Results: Major depressive disorder was associated with a higher age-corrected brain age gap than controls (mean difference +2.0 years, Cohen's d -0.289). Gaps were absent before the mid-30s and reached +6.8 years in those aged 55 and older before site adjustment (4.3 years after). Conclusion: Structural brain aging in depression is age-dependent and strongest in a clinically vulnerable phenotype, consistent with but not establishing neuroprogression models.

cards.title: Cross-cohort validation of EEG biomarkers using a pre-registered three-criterion framework: a demonstration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
cards.post: Aim: To develop and demonstrate a pre-registered three-criterion framework for identifying EEG features that show discrimination, reliability and cross-cohort consistency in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Methods: Eighteen EEG features assessed across three cohorts: a home-recorded ALS cohort with 170 controls, a clinic-recorded ALS cohort of eight patients, and a healthy test-retest reference of 60 participants, with permutation and bootstrap robustness testing. Results: Gamma power, theta power and spectral entropy met all three criteria. Cross-cohort differences in reliability, such as relative beta power (ICC 0.09 at home versus 0.93 in clinic), were large relative to the disease signal, and the selected set was sensitive to sample composition. Conclusion: Recording setting and protocol differences can outweigh disease-associated EEG signal, so cross-cohort validation is essential before biomarker translation.

cards.title: Neural Entropy Pattern : An EEG Representation for Predicting Depression Therapy Outcomes.
cards.post: Aim: Whether a multichannel EEG entropy representation can predict antidepressant and rTMS treatment response before treatment begins. Methods: Neural Entropy Pattern of ten entropy measures across 19 channels and five bands plus broadband; twelve deep and seven shallow models tested on SSRI (n = 30) and rTMS (n = 61) datasets under LOSO and five-fold cross-validation. cards.title: Synergistic contributions of periodic and aperiodic cortical activity to motor recovery prediction after stroke.
cards.post: Aim: To test whether periodic and aperiodic resting EEG components predict motor recovery after chronic stroke. Methods: Resting-state EEG (1 minute) recorded at admission and discharge with a portable system in 41 chronic stroke patients, parameterised with spectral decomposition and used in stepwise regression and classification. cards.title: The influence of the 1/f component in non-invasive transcranial electrical stimulation waveforms on neural oscillations
cards.post: Aim: To determine whether including the 1/f component in transcranial electrical stimulation waveforms changes neural oscillations compared with stimulation without it. Methods: Randomised, sham-controlled crossover study in 20 analysed healthy young adults receiving 20 minutes of individual spectrum-characteristic stimulation, aperiodic-removed stimulation or sham, with resting EEG before and after and generalised linear mixed models. Results: Aperiodic-removed stimulation significantly increased alpha power compared with sham, whereas individual spectrum stimulation did not differ from sham. Neither condition altered the aperiodic exponent or offset. Conclusion: Contrary to expectations, the spectral composition of personalised waveforms, including the 1/f component, may be a relevant parameter warranting further study.

cards.title: Multi-receptor whole-brain modeling reveals affinity-driven chemoarchitectural mechanism of virtual atomoxetine action.
cards.post: Aim: To explain how atomoxetine reshapes whole-brain dynamics by linking multi-receptor adrenergic and dopaminergic organisation to resting-state functional connectivity. Methods: Pharmacological resting-state fMRI under atomoxetine and placebo combined with a whole-brain model incorporating cortical adrenergic and dopaminergic receptor expression, using receptor similarity and forward simulation. cards.title: Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling: Brain and Cardiac Effective Connectivity
cards.post: Aim: To introduce Embodied Dynamic Causal Modelling for estimating effective connectivity across the cortex, brainstem and heart. Methods: Extension of generative causal modelling with a closed-loop brainstem cardiac neural mass model including five brainstem nuclei, a thalamic relay and the sinoatrial node, jointly inverted with simultaneous EEG and ECG during an auditory Go/No-Go task. Results: The framework distinguished granular from agranular microcircuit hypotheses within the viscero-sensorimotor hierarchy and recovered time-varying synaptic efficacy with latent neuronal dynamics across anticipation, target and inhibition windows. Conclusion: Linking neural and cardiac signals in one generative architecture moves brain-heart research beyond correlation and offers a way to test embodied inference theories.

cards.title: The biological basis underlying the local brain functional changes of taVNS in treating major depressive disorder: An imaging transcriptomics study.
cards.post: Aim: Whether the functional brain changes produced by eight weeks of taVNS in major depression map onto specific gene expression and neurotransmitter receptor patterns. Methods: Prospective single-arm longitudinal cohort of 122 patients with MDD, resting-state fMRI before and after 8 weeks of taVNS; ALFF and ReHo change correlated with HAMD-17 change, linked to Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression via LASSO and to 32 PET receptor maps. Results: 86 participants (70.5%) met the response criterion. Gene expression predicted ReHo response better (R2 = 0.309) than ALFF response (R2 = 0.174); ALFF linked to cation channel and NMDA pathways, ReHo to microglial and interferon signalling, with the strongest receptor correlation for GABA-A density in ReHo. Without a control group, the improvement cannot be attributed to taVNS itself. Conclusion: taVNS-associated functional changes show spatial enrichment for distinct synaptic and neuroimmune pathways, offering candidate molecular correlates, though the single-arm design limits efficacy inference.

cards.title: Temporal imprecision of the self in drug-free psychosis: Abnormal infraslow phase dynamics and brain complexity
cards.post: Aim: Whether infraslow brain dynamics in drug-free early psychosis show temporal imprecision linked to self-disturbance. Methods: Resting-state fMRI in 31 drug-free early psychosis patients (scanned before and after medication) and 31 healthy controls; sample entropy and instantaneous peak frequency computed in regions of interoceptive, exteroceptive and mental self-processing. cards.title: Brain-heart decoupling in somatic depression: Desynchronization between salience network neuropsychological connectivity and heart rate variability.
cards.post: Aim: Whether salience network oscillations and heart rate variability are coupled differently in somatic depression than in non-somatic depression and healthy controls. cards.title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of interoceptive conceptual processing in the human brain.
cards.venue: Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior
cards.post: Aim: How the strength of interoceptive meaning in verbs shapes the spatiotemporal neural dynamics of conceptual processing. Methods: MEG study with 16 participants in a lexical decision task using high- and low-interoceptive verbs; time-frequency analysis, representational similarity analysis, descriptive source reconstruction and cardiac variability measures. Results: High-interoceptive verbs elicited greater low-beta power (15-21 Hz) at 96-176 ms over right temporal sensors, with larger responses linked to lower short-term cardiac variability. Conclusion: Interoceptive strength is a distinct dimension of conceptual organisation, and accessing interoceptive meaning recruits neural dynamics tied to regulating internal bodily states.

cards.title: Dissociating Early Heartbeat-Evoked Afferent Gating From Late Associative Failure in Post-Anoxic Coma
cards.post: Aim: Whether the heartbeat-evoked response can separate viable from non-viable cortical function in comatose patients after cardiac arrest. Methods: Multicentre EEG and ECG from 150 comatose post-cardiac arrest patients (discovery n = 100, validation n = 50); sLORETA source localisation and Hilbert-Huang transform with empirical mode decomposition of early (150-300 ms) and late (350-500 ms) post-R-peak windows. Results: Good outcome was linked to a preserved frontocentral deflection near 200 ms localised to the anterior cingulate and anterior insula, with high instantaneous energy and phase alignment. cards.post: Aim: Whether prior psychedelic use and mental health diagnosis are associated with attitudes towards psychedelic-assisted therapy. Methods: Cross-sectional anonymous online convenience survey of 99 adults aged 21 or older recruited via social media and text messages; t tests and Fisher exact tests comparing groups by prior psychedelic use, diagnosis and healthcare-worker status. cards.title: Psilocybin modulates nucleus accumbens activity via astrocytic transcriptional regulation.
cards.post: Aim: How psilocybin and related tryptamines modulate inhibitory tone in the nucleus accumbens, and whether astrocytes contribute. Methods: Behavioural drug discrimination, in vivo neurochemistry, ex vivo whole-cell recordings, cell-type-specific GABA measures, ChIP-qPCR and calcium imaging in rodent nucleus accumbens tissue. Results: Psilocybin-like tryptamines increased NAc neuronal activity and reduced extracellular GABA. Psilocin reduced tonic GABA current without affecting miniature IPSCs; psilocybin lowered astrocytic GABA, raised NFATc4 and ALDH5A1, and its calcium responses were blocked by 5-HT2A antagonism. Conclusion: The authors propose psilocybin modulates mesolimbic inhibitory tone through astrocyte-associated transcriptional regulation of GABA homeostasis, a mechanism linked to 5-HT2A signalling.

cards.title: Mapping Endogenous Psychedelic Chemistry: Indolethylamine N -Methyltransferase (INMT) Localizes Proximal to the Golgi Apparatus of Human Neurons
cards.post: Aim: To characterise INMT, the DMT-producing enzyme, at the protein level in human neurons and locate it within the cell. Methods: Validated anti-INMT antibody and immunocytochemistry in human iPSC-derived neurons, co-localising INMT, DMT-like and 5-HT2A receptor signals with the Golgi apparatus. Results: INMT localised close to other DMT biosynthetic enzymes at the cytosolic face of the cis-Golgi network across multiple Golgi phenotypes. DMT-like and 5-HT2A immunoreactivity partly localised near the Golgi. Conclusion: The cis-Golgi network may be a microdomain for psychedelic tryptamine biosynthesis, possibly creating a local pool of DMT accessing intracellular 5-HT2A receptors.

cards.title: Long-term dysregulation of histone acetylation, BDNF expression, and the hippocampal transcriptome in adult rats exhibiting a depressive-like phenotype following repeated chlorpyrifos exposure
cards.post: Aim: In this study, we use a rat model of occupational-like CPF exposure associated with a chronic depressive phenotype to investigate underlying molecular mechanisms. Methods: Adult rats received CPF (5 mg/kg/day) for 21 days. We used chromatin immunoprecipitation to assay histone 3 lysine 9 acetylation (H3K9ac) occupancy at the Bdnf promoter IV. Results: H3K9ac levels at the Bdnf promoter IV were significantly reduced in CPF rats, accompanied by a concomitant reduction in BDNF protein expression. Conclusion: Overall, this study indicates persistent epigenetic and transcriptional dysregulation associated with reduced hippocampal BDNF and alterations in neuronal plasticity-related pathways linked to a long-term depressive-like phenotype following CPF exposure.

cards.title: Rotigotine Behenate ameliorates depression in Parkinson's disease through NF-κB-mediated anti-inflammation and BDNF-mediated neuroprotection.
cards.post: Background: Depression in Parkinson's disease (DPD) is a prevalent non-motor complication that currently lacks effective targeted therapy. Methods: We established a combined MPTP/CUMS model in male C57BL/6 mice, which induced a higher incidence of depression and more stable depressive-like phenotypes than MPTP-only modeling and closely recapitulated clinical DPD pathology. Results: Behavioral assays demonstrated that ROTB ameliorated both motor dysfunction and depressive-like behavior and restored regional neurotransmitter balance, whereas fluoxetine-included solely as an efficacy comparator for the depressive-like phenotype-did not improve motor symptoms. Mechanistically, ROTB suppressed NF-κB/NLRP3-mediated neuroinflammation and activated the BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/Akt/GSK-3β cascade, elevating synaptic protein levels and reversing dendritic spine loss. Conclusion: In summary, ROTB alleviates DPD through NF-κB-mediated anti-inflammation and BDNF-mediated neuroprotection, offering preclinical evidence for DPD therapy.

cards.title: From Intrinsic Topography to Cognitive Prediction: Benchmarking Approaches to Personalized Cortical Parcellation.
cards.venue: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
cards.post: Background: Personalized functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) adapts cortical parcellations to individual functional anatomy. Methods: Using the Human Connectome Project Young Adult dataset (N = 947), we compared five personalized parcellation methods and a standard group-level atlas. Results: We also examined whether connectivity and topographic features were associated with and predicted general intelligence (g). Using kernel ridge regression, functional connectivity significantly predicted g, with the group atlas yielding the highest predictive accuracy, consistent with a potential advantage of cross-individual spatial correspondence for edge-wise prediction. Conclusion: We conclude that personalized parcellation approaches are associated with distinct trade-offs in spatial correspondence, topographic variability, and downstream predictive utility.

cards.title: Gene discovery and pleiotropic architecture of multidimensional pain in a genome-wide association study of >1.2 million individuals.
cards.post: Background: Chronic pain is highly prevalent worldwide, yet its genetic architecture remains to be fully elucidated. Methods: Here we leveraged data from 1,235,695 European-ancestry individuals across three biobanks. Results: In a meta-analytic genome-wide association study of multidimensional pain (MP), we identified 343 independent loci, 92 of which were new pain associations. Conclusion: This study expands our knowledge of the genetics of pain and its pathogenesis, highlighting the importance of its pleiotropy with multiple disorders and elucidating its multi-omic pathophysiology.

cards.title: Semaglutide for the Treatment of Obesity in Children 6 to <12 Years of Age.
cards.venue: The New England journal of medicine
cards.post: Background: Once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide is approved for the treatment of obesity in adolescents and adults, but data for its use in young children are lacking. Methods: We conducted a phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving children (6 to <12 years of age) with obesity. Results: At week 68, the mean percent change in BMI was -13.5% with semaglutide and 2.7% with placebo (estimated between-group difference, -16.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -19.4 to -12.9; P<0.001). Conclusion: Among children (6 to <12 years of age) with obesity, treatment with semaglutide for 68 weeks resulted in a significantly greater mean percent reduction in BMI than placebo.

cards.title: Increased signal diversity/complexity of spontaneous EEG, but not evoked EEG responses, in ketamine-induced psychedelic state in humans
cards.post: Background: How and to what extent electrical brain activity reflects pharmacologically altered states and contents of consciousness, is not well understood. Methods: Therefore, we investigated whether measures of evoked and spontaneous electroencephalographic (EEG) signal diversity are altered by sub-anaesthetic levels of ketamine compared to normal wakefulness, and how these measures relate to subjective experience. Results: Although no significant difference was found in TMS-evoked complexity (PCI) between the sub-anaesthetic ketamine condition and normal wakefulness, all measures of spontaneous EEG signal diversity (LZc, ACE, SCE) showed significantly increased values in the sub-anaesthetic ketamine condition. This increase in signal diversity correlated with subjective assessment of altered states of consciousness. Conclusion: Thus, sub-anaesthetic ketamine may increase the complexity of the conscious content and the brain activity underlying it, while the level or general capacity for consciousness remains largely unaffected.

cards.title: Neural Sources and Underlying Mechanisms of Neural Responses to Heartbeats, and their Role in Bodily Self-consciousness: An Intracranial EEG Study
cards.post: Background: Recent research has shown that heartbeat-evoked potentials (HEPs), brain activity in response to heartbeats, are a useful neural measure for investigating the functional role of brain-body interactions in cognitive processes including self-consciousness. Methods: In 2 experiments, using intracranial electroencephalography (EEG), we investigated (1) the neural sources of HEPs, (2) the underlying mechanisms for HEP generation, and (3) the functional role of HEPs in bodily self-consciousness. Results: In Experiment-1, we found that shortly after the heartbeat onset, phase distributions across single trials were significantly concentrated in 10% of the recording sites, mainly in the insula and the operculum, but also in other regions including the amygdala and fronto-temporal cortex. Conclusion: Collectively, these results provide novel and solid electrophysiological evidence on the neural sources and underlying mechanisms of HEPs, and their functional role in self-consciousness.
